author: Robert Jordan
introFa: کتاب «Lord of Chaos» نوشته Robert Jordan یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Lord of Chaos»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 1 The old goblin slouched on his throne glaring at the thantor that guarded the tunnel to his left. He knew another thantor guarded the other side, just beyond sight. He had endured more than two thousand years. During that time, he had survived two encounters with The Ghost and another two with the feline god. He knew he had been lucky. Now he found himself a prisoner in his own home. Thantors. He hated them. They would not let him leave until they heard from their true master. The old goblin knew that the thantors were not here to guard him against harm. They stood their posts to keep him in this room. Even the little runt, Brek, his slave, had more freedom than he did. The slave had two rooms in which to get bored, this one, and the one where his sleeping mat lay. His own guards were stationed in the two rooms adjacent to the throne room. They would come if he called for them, but not voluntarily. They were too afraid of these cursed black insects, the thantors, to come here willingly. His fingers absently traced the ancient rune on the wall beside him. The presence of The Ghost felt stronger to him. He could remember when the touch of the rune caused him great discomfort. He had craved it anyway. Now it was a source of pleasure. I wish something would come to destroy those things, he thought. Seconds later, the thantor guarding the left tunnel burst into white flames and disintegrated to ash. The goblin slid to the edge of his seat. A wicked sharp-toothed grin replaced his glower. The second thantor entered the room and encored the fate of the first. The goblin waited. He knew that whoever killed the thantors would probably end his luck and his life. He accepted this. His life had been long enough. Death would be a welcome change from his current situation. A third thantor entered the chamber. “Die!” the old goblin cackled.

Again, the white flame struck adding a third pile of ash to the cavern floor. “Hehe! Yes!” The goblin now stood on the rock ledge in front of his throne. His hand constantly waving onward whatever waited in the tunnel. “Come in, already,” it cackled. “I already have,” a soft voice said from behind the goblin. The goblin slid off his throne and slowly turned. A young black-eyed elf sat on the back of his throne. The goblin recognized The Ghost immediately. He wore the same type clothing he always wore, a dark green cloak and a fur loincloth. The goblin marveled slightly at the lack of scars on the elf's body. He knew there should be scars around both ankles. The goblin licked his lips remembering the blood he had sucked from the elf's feet when they adorned his throne. The elf had taken the bow that hung on the wall and had it resting across his lap. The goblin grinned. “The Ghost returns. Have you come to kill me?” “No. I want my bow and a young goblin.” “The whole goblin?” the old goblin sneered. The elf nodded. “Alive and healthy.” “And what do I get?” The elf grinned. “I can return those thantors as easily as I destroyed them.” The old goblin frowned. He glanced at the three piles of ash, then asked, “How young?” “My children are ten seasons. I need a goblin near that age.” “You sound as if you want to raise it. Guard!” A moment later, a goblin ran into the chamber. He saw the elf seated on the back of the throne and drew his sword. “No, you fool! You wouldn't be able to get close to him. He would kill you before you could take two steps. Bring me young Brek.” The guard scampered from the chamber as a feline shape took form in the middle of the room. Rachk'sha glanced at the goblin then bowed before the elf. “My triplets will be receiving their inheritance soon,” the elf remarked. “I truly hope there will be no uninvited visitors.” “There won't,” purred Rachk'sha. The elf nodded and watched the guard return with a young goblin. Ky slid off the throne and met the young goblin in the middle of the chamber. He circled the goblin and said, “He'll do. Do goblins

have coming of age rituals?” “No. What are you going to do with him?” the old goblin asked. “Make him immortal. You won't see me again,” he added as he took hold of Brek's arm. The old goblin rushed forward. “Tell the cat to leave before you go. He will listen to you.” Ky stared at the old goblin a moment then nodded. “Leave, Rachk'sha. As soon as you finish what you wanted to do.” Ky and Brek vanished. Rachk'sha grinned as he approached the old goblin. “Come. Give me a tour of these fine caverns. I've never had the pleasure of a full tour. I wish to meet every adorable goblin in your tribe.” The old goblin led Rachk'sha into a passage as he asked, "What did he mean by immortal?" "The Ghost is probably going to make a god of your little slave. The Ghost's magic will make him immortal, just like it made you immortal," Rachk'sha hissed, his tail lashing angrily. "I'm immortal?" the old goblin gasped, stopping in the middle of the passageway. "Don't think yourself so special," Rachk'sha snarled, pushing the goblin forward. "You are a freak, an accident. You are immortal because The Ghost's magic made you so when you escaped being killed by him. He didn't even know he did it." As they walked through the passage, Rachk'sha gently brushed against the goblin and muttered, "All are your enemies here. You must destroy them." "What are you mumbling?" the old goblin asked as they entered the first chamber. "Nothing," Rachk'sha purred. The old goblin looked around the room. Two goblin guards stood at the mouth of the passage and several more sat around a fire gnawing on the remains of a rancid rabbit. The old goblin's eyes widened as he screamed. He tore into the guards with clawed hands and sharp teeth. The other goblins in the room scurried to the far corner, trying desperately to become part of the wall. With the guards dead, he charged into the goblins across the room, ripping out their throats with his teeth. He craved the taste of their blood. He reveled in the feel of their necks ripping open between his teeth. His breathing became quick and raspy as he turned to the next passage. Rachk'sha, forgotten by the old goblin, chuckled softly as he followed. Through chamber after chamber the old goblin slaughtered all he encountered. The farther through the maze of

tunnels he moved, the more his body was bathed in the blood of his kin. Hours later, Rachk'sha followed as the old goblin stumbled into the throne room. The crazed look slowly faded from the goblin's eyes as he stood panting before the throne. "Very impressive," Rachk'sha said. "What did you make me do?" "You forget so easily. Let me remind you." Rachk'sha gestured and the passages that led from the chamber began to fill with corpses. The piles of torn goblin bodies clogged both passages becoming macabre bars to the old goblin's throne room. "No!" the old goblin screamed as he fell to his knees. Several corpses settled around the chamber as Rachk'sha explained, "I'm sorry about these in here, but they wouldn't fit in the passageways. Don't worry about anyone discovering what you've done today," he added as he stomped his foot. Dust and rock fell from the ceiling as the earth shook. "It seems the goblin caverns have all collapsed in an earthquake." "Kill me! Why won't you kill me?" the old goblin pleaded. "You are a creation of The Ghost's magic. It would take me a great deal of time to find a way to kill you. Unfortunately, you had The Ghost tell me to leave when I finished, so I must go now." Rachk'sha's laughter faded with his body. The old goblin crawled to his throne, climbed into it and sobbed. Time passed and the sobs became interrupted by short bursts of laughter. Soon, the laughter dominated and the goblin glared at the corpses lying around the chamber and packing the passageways. He pointed to the closest and yelled, "You weren't good enough for the likes of me!" He pointed to another, "You were worthless! You needed to be killed!" The old goblin descended his throne and dragged the closest corpse to the wall. He ripped into the abdomen with his clawed fingers. Using the blood from the corpse, he drew the rune for 'spawn' over the older 'ghost' rune. “I am no longer goblin chief. Now, I am Ghostspawn. I will find new followers to honor me. Then I will conquer whatever I want,” he ranted. He scampered to a passageway and began to pull a goblin corpse from the pile. The bodies were wedged tightly together and it took him a long time to finally free one. He glared at the grotesque wall blocking his escape as he stood panting from the exertion. “There's no need to hurry,” he raved. “I am immortal. I have forever to finish.” He rested, then fought to pull the next corpse from the clog. After a while, the task became easier. The bodies did not cling to each other as greedily now that he had extracted a few. His

progress became quicker as he worked his way into the passage. Hour after hour passed. More and more dead littered the chamber floor. Through the rest of the night and most of the next morning, he removed the remains of his kin from the passage. Finally, he had cleared enough to find the packed dirt and rubble caused by the collapse of the goblin caves. He stacked two of the bodies on a side wall and used them as a chair to rest for a while. Then, slowly, he began to dig through the cave-in.

2 Herr William sipped his hot chocolate. He glanced at the discarded suit crumpled on the floor in front of the sunroom door. Moments before, Micah filled that suit. Ky had come for the Old Man and Micah. The Old Man was the first to go. Herr William stared into the steam from his mug remembering their last conversation. "Thank you for all you've done for us these past twenty years," the Old Man said. "Thank you as well. I find it impossible to believe that you are leaving." "I'll be back to visit as soon as I recover. Stay with Little Ky for us, please. We have to make sure his body is ready to receive him and then find his soul-prison." "Take as long as you need. He will be well cared for." They clasped arms and the Old Man quickly turned away. Herr William understood. In twenty years, they had become very close friends. He wanted to turn away himself, to deny the reality of the situation. Instead, he watched the Old Man step into the small glowing portal in front of the sunroom door, then vanish. Micah had been in the sunroom saying goodbye to Little Ky. Herr William remembered thinking it strange that Ky would ask for him. Micah stepped through the door wiping tears from his cheeks. Ky touched Micah's hand and he instantly reverted to the ten-year-old

skinny little kid that Herr William had adopted twenty years prior. Micah's suit, which fit the large man Micah had grown into, fell to the floor at his feet, now way too large to find purchase on the small body. Apparently, the little black-eyed elf had patience for only one farewell. Herr William had less than a second to remember the shocked expression on Micah's face before Ky pushed him into the portal. Then Ky himself stepped through the portal. A moment later, the portal was gone and Little Ky stood in the doorway smiling. "Micah too?" was all Herr William could think to say. "He asked my father if he could. Neither of us thought he would be able to, though." Little Ky stepped over the suit left by Micah and walked to the sofa. "At least I'll have some time with you," Herr William had said. "I'll make us some hot chocolate." Herr William remembered leaning against the door frame near the kitchen watching Little Ky seated on the sofa flipping through an Austrian history book. He turned away long enough to mix the chocolate. He carried the two mugs into the room and froze halfway to the sofa. The edges of the boy's body seemed hazy. At first, Herr William thought it was a trick of the light, but Little Ky had noticed it too. The boy stared at the hand raised before him. He looked across the room at Herr William. "I'll miss you..." The uniform he wore slowly settled on the sofa and floor as the body within faded. Herr William stood staring at the uniform with moisture-blurred vision. They were all gone now. "I'll miss you, too," he muttered as he slowly walked to the easy chair. Their departure seemed so long ago, though only minutes had passed. He barely remembered placing Little Ky's chocolate beside the history book before seating himself. He finished his own drink and stared at the neglected mug on the table. Slowly, he gathered the two mugs and cleaned them in the kitchen. When he returned, he collected Micah's suit and neatly folded it, setting it on the end of the coffee table. Then, he did the same with Little Ky's uniform. On top of the uniform, he placed the history book. He stood guard over his stack of memoirs as he searched the room. He found two books on the small end-table beside the easy chair. A torn piece of loose-leaf paper marked the Old Man's page in the top book. Nodding, he collected the books and added them to the pile. He picked up the uniforms and books and shuffled to the door, his eyes firmly focused on his destination. There were too many memories here. He could feel them creeping up behind him as he crossed the room. He felt if he turned back, he would never be able to

leave. “I'll miss you. All of you,” he said as he shut the cottage door and walked down the flagstone path towards the school. He glanced through the garden to where just the day before, the small black-eyed elf emerged from the funeral pyre. Yesterday. The end had come so quickly. His shoulders sagged as he climbed the stone steps that led into the foyer of the school. Herr William barely nodded to his secretary as he passed through the outer office into his own. He hesitated a moment in the doorway, then walked to the reddish brown leather chair and sank into it, still holding his souvenirs. He set the uniforms and books on the side of his desk before pressing the call button on his phone. "Yes, Herr William," a female voice replied. "Frau Schmidt, please bring me the file of choir director applicants." "Right away, Herr William." As he waited for the file, he slid a piece of paper from his top desk drawer and began writing his retirement letter. Frau Schmidt entered the room carrying a manila folder as he finished. “Here is the folder you requested, Herr William,” she said placing it on his desk. “Is there anything else you need?” “Yes. Kindly type this for me,” he said handing her the letter. “Also, please ask Herr Jensen to come. One moment...” Herr William opened the folder and began flipping through the applications. He selected two, and handed them to Frau Schmidt. “Contact these two and see if they are still available.” “You're,” she swallowed, “retiring?” Herr William smiled. “It's about time. Don't you agree? I'm seventy-years-old and have been working here at the school for over fifty of those years.” “What about the Old Man and the boy? Your replacement may not be as accommodating as you've been.” “They are both gone, as is Micah,” Herr William said, involuntarily glancing at the pile he collected from the cottage. “I'm recommending Herr Jensen as my replacement. First, though, I have to replace him and Herr Micah. I want everything to be in order when I leave.” “I'll make the calls right away, Herr William.” She walked to the door and paused. “You will be missed.” “Thank you, Frau Schmidt. I'm not gone yet, though. You can miss me later.”

Frau Schmidt smiled and left the office. Herr William leaned back and rested his eyes. The intercom buzzer and the voice of Frau Schmidt startled him awake with the message that Herr Jensen had arrived. He pressed the button on the phone and requested, "Send him in, please." "Also, both applicants are still available. I took the liberty to schedule them for tomorrow." "Thank you, Frau Schmidt." Herr Jensen entered the room. He was a tall, broadly built man with piercing blue eyes and thick dirty-blond hair. He appeared to be quite intimidating, but Herr William knew he had a kind heart. Herr William stood to greet him. "Please, have a seat." "Thank you." After both seated themselves, Herr William explained, "I asked you to meet me because I've recommended you as my replacement. Frau Schmidt has already set up an interview with your replacement." "I am greatly honored you would consider me, Herr William. Thank you! What if the board does not approve your recommendation?" Herr William smiled, "There's no need to worry about that. They will approve you. They know as well as I do that you would be best for the job." Herr Jensen returned the smile. "I will be as hospitable to the Old Man, Micah and Little Ky as you have been, so there is no need to discuss that." "That is not an issue," Herr William said standing. "All three left today." Herr Jensen rose from his seat. "I'm sorry their departure was so sudden. I know you cared a great deal for all three of them." "I think it is better that way," Herr William said as he led Herr Jensen to the door. "This way I don't have the pain of anticipation. Good day to you, Herr Jensen." "And to you, Sir." After Herr Jensen left, Herr William began deciding how best to pack his belongings. He had resided in this office for twenty- three years and had collected quite a bit of memories in that time. Sighing, he pressed the intercom button. "Yes, Herr William?" "I'll need a few boxes, Frau Schmidt. Would you assign someone to gather them for me, please?" "Right away, Sir."

He returned to his chair and started searching through his desk. Many of the items he organized and left in the drawers. Those that had personal meaning he began to stack neatly beside Micah's suit. Old photographs, letters which he quickly scanned that brought a slight smile to his visage, a tattered hard-bound diary, a handwritten scrap of music – all these he added to his pile. He had just finished the second drawer when a knock resounded from the door. "Enter," he called as he closed the drawer. Frau Schmidt entered carrying two empty boxes. She placed them on the floor beside Herr William's chair and said, "We are looking for a couple more. Is there anything else you need?" Herr William afforded her a smile and shook his head. "Just some time to get this stuff together. Please let me know when it is time for dinner. I may be distracted and forget to check the clock." "Of course, Herr William," she said as she left the office. Herr William took a deep breath and organized what he had taken from the first two drawers into one of the boxes and opened the next drawer. He had two weeks to vacate the office. He removed items from the drawer one at a time. He lingered on each item, soaking in the past, savoring each memory. Halfway through the contents of the drawer, he found a crumpled piece of looseleaf paper crammed into the back corner. He placed it on his desk and carefully smoothed it. Tears slowly escaped his eyes as he read the faded pencil scratchings. August 1987 Dear Herr Wiliam and teechers, Thank you for adapting me and leting me come to your school. I will really work hard. You realy made me happy bringing me heer. Love, Micah. Herr William read the note many times, smoothing the paper a little more after each read. Then he folded it and placed it safely inside Little Ky's history book. "I will miss you, my son," he whispered as he closed the book. "My one regret is that I never told you." The book remained on the center of his desk and Herr William returned to the note every so often. Sometimes he read it, other times he stared at it as memories of Micah passed through his mind. He had just put it away again when the buzzer sounded on the intercom.

"Fifteen minutes until dinner, Sir." He leaned back into his chair a moment staring at the phone. Taking a deep breath, he pressed the call button and replied, "Thank you, Frau Schmidt. I will be out shortly." He looked into the box he had been packing and found it nearly empty. "I have two weeks," he muttered as he stepped over it and walked from the room.

3 The council room had changed. Two small tables had replaced the council table. The room now doubled as a dining area and school, complete with library. It also served as an informal meeting place for the members of the Combined Council. Sharing the struggle with Rachk'sha at the farm gave the members a nostalgic bond there. On any given day, one could find members of both The Nine and the Council of Darkness meeting or visiting at the farm. Karnak visited with Archos and Delmaria at one table as the triplets and Aemir sat at the other table preparing for their journey into the forest behind the farm. "You don't think Ky would have forgotten our plans?" Karnak asked. "I'm sure he remembers," Delmaria answered as she made sure each of their mugs were full. "I believe the schedule is not as important to him as it would be to you." "Aye," Archos added, smiling at Delmaria. "If he shows up today, you should consider yourself lucky." Karnak straightened, his face turning towards the front of the farmhouse. "A goblin," he said quietly. "Stay seated, Ky II," Archos said as he stood. "It's only one goblin. No need to get excited." "It's coming this way, Archos. Might as well wait here for it. The elves at the other table will die of curiosity if they don't see for themselves what's happening," Karnak added. The four elves forgot all their preparations and watched the doorway intently as Archos returned to his seat. They craned their

necks to get the best view of the doorway until Ky finally entered escorting a young goblin into the room. He led the goblin to Karnak. "A present for you," Ky said quietly. "What would you have me do with it?" "The Council of Darkness needs some replacements," Ky answered as he sat beside Karnak. Karnak nodded slowly. "My council does have some empty seats, but why would you bring me a goblin whelp with no training? I don't have the time now to train him and neither do you. We have the thantor problem we must deal with." "Someone else will start his training. That's why I chose a whelp. He'll train with the triplets until we complete what we need to do." "But he's a goblin!" Tal complained. "And he really stinks," Ky II added. "I guess you need to clean him up then. The two of you take him to the back and bathe him," Ky instructed. "Brek not like water!" Ky stared at the goblin for a moment. "Okay, no water." Ky's hand flared intensely with white-hot flame. "I'll just burn the dirt off you." "Brek like water now! Come, elves, show Brek water. Please!" Brek pleaded as he scampered to the other table. "Ewww." Ky II slid off his chair. "Let's get it over with, Tal. The sooner we finish the sooner we don't have to smell him anymore." Tal quickly stood and hustled to the door as he called, "This way, Brek." Brek gave Ky a wide berth as he scampered after Tal. Ky II followed and muttered, "I think I prefer the burn-the-dirt-off method," as he passed his father. Karnak waited until the three had left the room, then quietly asked, "Will your children treat the goblin fairly?" "Listen," Ky whispered. Eleana and Aemir continued making preparations at the other table, not daring to draw the attention of Karnak and Ky. "This is going to lengthen our stay in the forest. We'll need to make him clothes as well," Eleana explained, giving the long-knife she was polishing more attention than was necessary. "Goblins don't wear clothes,” Aemir said, keeping his voice low and polishing a longsword. “Well, they do if they are going into battle. But that's only when they know they are going. Even then, they only wear a couple crude bits of armor." "He's one of us now. He has to be like us, and we wear clothes." Eleana's kept her voice low, but stole a furtive glance at the

table where Ky and Karnak sat. Her face grew serious as she looked at Aemir and said, “Brek will probably be going with us. We need to make sure he feels he is one of us.” She waited until Aemir nodded, then picked up a sharpening stone and began working on her other long-knife. Karnak nodded. "Eleana is a good leader. Are you ready to begin hunting the thantors?" "No. I want to wait until they are on their way into the forest." Laena entered the room and asked, "Is Tobit available? Ky II needs him." "I'll send for him," Archos said. "I wonder what they did to that goblin." "I'll check," Ky said as he left the table. Ky entered the small room that housed the farm's bathing tub. Brek, frowning miserably, sat in the tub while Ky II and Tal worked frantically to scrub him clean. "What's wrong?" Ky asked. Ky II said, "I'll be right back," and led Ky into the next room. "I checked him for injuries like I did for Simon. I'm not sure, but I think one of his lungs is damaged. That's why I asked for Tobit. I figured he might know for sure." Ky grinned. "Archos has sent for him." Ky II returned his father's grin and walked back to the small room to help Tal. Tobit arrived a few minutes later. "What does this victim need from me?" Tobit asked as he entered the bathing room. "Check his chest," Ky II answered. "It might be nothing, but I wanted to make sure." "First Brek has to get in water, now Brek victim," the goblin complained. "Next, Brek will be dead goblin." Tobit laughed. "My last victim told me my examinations tickled. Maybe you can verify that for me." He placed his hand on the young goblins chest and searched for injuries. "Good thing you sent for me, Ky II. You are going to be tired when I finish, Brek. The good news is that you'll live a lot longer." "That just means elves make Brek get in water more," the goblin complained as he unsuccessfully fought with the Ky II over the rag scrubbing his ear. Tobit concentrated his magic and sent it into the goblin. "I'll share a little secret with you, Brek. They won't like that I told you this, but, I have to do it. If you get into water more often, you will not have to stay in it so long." "Brek not understand."

Tobit finished healing Brek's lung and explained, "The more often you clean yourself, the easier it is to stay clean. If you wait a long time, then you will have to be in the water a long time." "Why'd you tell him that? You're spoiling all our fun!" Ky II complained. "Yeah, now we won't be able to make him miserable as much," Tal added. Tobit laughed. "Is Brek going with you on your training mission?" Ky II nodded. "Yeah. We have to train him since dad and Karnak are busy." "When you finish with him, I'll train Eleana how to heal him if the need arises. I'll wait in the council room." Tobit smiled and left the elves to their chore. "Brek wonders why he is being trained." "I think," Tal offered, "you are being prepared to become a member of The Council of Darkness." Ky II nodded. "We've got to make a god out of a goblin." "Brek will outlaw water when he is a god!" Ky II and Tal laughed. By the time they finished with Brek, dinner was being served. They gave him an old tunic to wear and introduced him to Simon, Little Ky and Micah. Eleana was given the chore of teaching Brek table manners. He had never used an eating utensil and plunged his hand into the stew. “No, Brek! Use the spoon!” Eleana exclaimed. “Here, like this.” She demonstrated how to hold the spoon and showed him how to eat the stew from the bowl. She guided his hand for the first couple spoonfuls, then let him try it on his own. The little goblin learned fast and soon started using his spoon to scarf down Eleana's and Simon's stew. “Brek, you don't have to do that here,” Eleana explained as she pushed his spoon away. “If you want more, just ask.” “Brek want more.” Eleana shook her head. “That wasn't quite asking, Brek.” Tal said, “It's an improvement over what he was doing, though.” “He probably wouldn't want much more if he didn't try to wear half of it,” Ky II said as he pointed at Brek's tunic. “At least he's not getting it all over us,” Simon muttered. After the meal, Tobit took Eleana and Brek to Laena's common area to teach Eleana how to heal him if needed. Delmaria

had arrived by the time they finished and was preparing to read one of her journals. Eleana joined the other children on the floor in the reading area. “This is the journal that brought Daphnia to the farm,” Delmaria explained. “I promised to read it for her and Illya quite some time ago. So, if everyone is ready, I'll begin.” Delmaria Keep of Cragsguard Reign of King Taren VI Year 1406 E.H. I've known Ky nine months now. He is still very reticent to enter The Cracked Anvil, but I think my father is beginning to change that. He is also starting to get a reputation with the Cragsguard militia. More often than not, we would overhear them boasting about Ky's adventures in the canyon near town. It is even rumored that he has acquired quite a bit of respect, or fear for that matter, from the goblins. In the many times I've seen him, either here in town or at the farm, I've never seen him fear anything. Today would change that. Two days ago, Ky left Cragsguard with a little extra money after killing some goblins. The old alchemist across the square had heard he was in town and decided to wait at The Cracked Anvil for the day. I believe he wanted Ky to do some work for him as well. Ky never appeared. I understand he did not enter town beyond the guardhouse where he received his reward. He usually made the trip to Cragsguard only once a month and the poor alchemist returned to his shop feeling very disappointed. No one expected to see Ky today. So his arrival surprised us all. He burst through the door and ran behind the bar. My father, shocked at his behavior, could do no more than stand there gaping at him. “Illya! The farm! Help!” Four words and he darted out the door. I tried to catch him while my father started closing the inn. By the time I arrived at the town gate, he was out of sight. I asked the guards if he said anything to them and they told me he ran into town without a word and a minute later ran out the same way. I guess the captain of the guard read my concern because he followed me back to the inn.

My father told the captain what happened and he ran to acquire horses and a few militia for us. The old alchemist had seen the captain leave and also came over. After hearing what had happened, he said he would join us, and returned to his shop to get his medicine bag. Within the hour, my father, the alchemist and I met the captain and six volunteers from the militia at the stables. We mounted our horses and galloped out of town. I will never know how Ky arrived at the farm before us. I guess the cross-country route he takes is shorter. Anyway, he was there, hiding behind the barn. His eyes were wide and his entire body trembled. I went to calm him as the guards, my father and the alchemist climbed onto the porch. The guards had never seen Ky afraid and were very reluctant to enter the house. I guess they thought if something in there could scare Ky, it was extremely dangerous. "Unless they change their pattern, they will be here." "How is it you can track them? Thantors are usually untraceable." "I can see more than tracks now. It happened with my inheritance. "I see you found the knife," he said quietly as he approached Simon. "Help me find the other thantor you and Tal killed." Ky II guided Simon into the forest towards the thantor's corpse. He turned aside when the body came into view and sat beside a tree. Simon glanced at the thantor, then sat beside Ky II. "What's wrong?" Ky II asked, his voice almost a whisper. "Just wondering when I'll finally do something all the way right," Simon muttered. "You're getting better. It takes a bit of practice to work with weapons. They have to become a part of your hand or they won't help you much." "You, Tal and Eleana make it look so easy, though. I can't even hold onto it long enough to get to the fight." Ky II took the knife from Simon and played with it a few moments. "We were trained. Dad made sure we had the best training,

too. We rarely saw him, but we saw what he did for us all the time." Ky II paused and handed the knife back to Simon. "Symplex taught us how to use these. Tobit stayed with us during the training, healing the wounds Symplex would cause. I don't know how much you know about elves but we age differently from humans. It takes about eighty to a hundred turnings of the seasons for us to age a human year. We trained with Symplex for that long. Before that we trained with Selia." Simon slowly traced the runes along the knife's blade. "Do you think I'll be able to be as good as you?" "Oh, yeah," Ky II said grinning. "It won't be easy, but you are my dad's brother. You'll be different than he is, I think, but you'll be his equal when you've trained." Simon glanced at Ky II's hand. It had had flames dancing across it during the entire conversation. "What are you planning on burning?" he asked quietly. "Nothing. It's so Tal and Eleana can see where we are." "I'm ready to go back now. Thanks for talking with me." Ky II stood. "Thanks for keeping Tal alive." He walked to the thantor and began dragging it into the village with Simon walking beside him. "I'm going to let Eleana put you to sleep again," Ky II said quietly. "Because of the healing." Simon smiled and turned towards the fire while Ky II dragged the thantor to the pile of corpses. Simon handed Eleana her long-knife and returned to his section of the blanket. "Sleep well," Eleana whispered as she placed her palm on his forehead. Simon immediately succumbed to Eleana's sleep spell. -You sleep as well- Ky II thought. -Tal, Brek and I can handle the watch.- -Only if you promise to wake me if anything happens.- Eleana answered. -Yeah, yeah. Go to sleep.- Ky II thought as he settled himself at the edge of the camp. Eleana knew Ky II had no intention of waking her until morning but decided it would be best not to argue with him. She lay down beside Little Ky on the edge of the blanket and tried to pretend to sleep. The exertion from the healing soon exhausted her and she fell asleep in spite of her efforts to stay awake. Ky II let Brek continue to keep watch for about an hour. He knew the goblin would be tired as well and sent him to rest with the others. The forest slept as Tal and Ky II watched over their sleeping friends. Shortly before dawn, one of the sey emerged from the hut. She watched the group at the fire-pit for a while before quietly

approaching the thantor corpses. Tal smiled as she hissed in his direction and grabbed the arm of one of the thantors. She dragged it back into the hut and was not seen again. -I guess we should wake the others.- Tal thought as the sey disappeared into the hut. -The sooner we are out of this forest, the happier I'll be.- Ky II roused Eleana first, then the three of them woke the others. They quickly packed the blanket and the thantor heads Ky II had collected and headed northward. Their journey brought them to a barricade. Ky II stayed with the group and Tal and Eleana walked to it to investigate. They got close enough to determine that the barricade had been constructed along the bank of a stream when a volley of arrows struck the forest floor at their feet. "Come any farther and you all will be killed," warned an unseen elf. As Tal and Eleana stepped back, the barricade in front of them exploded into flames.

6 Taelann stood beside the table as Archos collected his scyring orb and Eleana's dragon. "Relax, Taelann," Archos soothed. "We can be there in seconds if they need us." Archos invoked the dragon and the sey village emerged within the mists of the orb before it. They watched as Eleana healed Aemir and placed a sleep spell on him before moving to Micah. Delmaria joined Archos and Taelann at the table. They watched the events until Ky II insisted that Eleana rest. Taelann sighed and asked, "I wonder how long their luck will hold out." "We didn't see the beginning of what happened, but from what we've seen, I believe luck had little to do with their success," Archos observed. Delmaria nodded agreement. "They handled the situation quite well." Taelann glanced at the sleepers in the orb and began pacing beside the table. "You're right," he muttered. "Daelann's loss is still too fresh in my heart. I don't think I could handle losing Aemir as well." Archos stepped into Taelann's path intercepting his pacing. "Ky's children have extensive training and can handle things. The triplets do anyway. Even if things go really bad, they will provide us the time to get to them if the need should arrive." Taelann returned to the table and sat in front of the orb watching the children sleeping in the fire's light. He saw Brek join them as Archos approached the table.

"It's best we not keep the connection open. We don't want them to feel that we need to watch their every move." Archos waved his hand over the orb and the mists obscured the scene. "The events lead me to think Aemir is not as trained as we assumed. Why don't you pay a visit to the shrine in Cragsguard and see what you can find out for us?" Taelann smiled at Archos. "It will be good to visit with Daelann. You'll know where to find me if anything comes up." "If you see my father," Delmaria said, "tell him I'll be by to visit some time tomorrow." "I will." Taelann left the table and walked to the portal. "If Aemir sends me a call for help, I'll let you know before I run off to the rescue." Archos laughed. "Please do. It's been a while since I've had the opportunity to run to the rescue. I wouldn't want to miss the chance." Taelann laughed as he passed through the portal. His laughter ended abruptly upon entering the kitchen of the Cracked Anvil. He returned to the council room. "The two of you should come to Cragsguard," he said to Archos and Delmaria. Archos and Delmaria followed Taelann through the portal. They stood gaping at the destruction they found in the kitchen. Broken shelves stood askew above scattered cookery littering the floor. The door to the back kitchen buckled and splintered under the weight of the partially collapsed ceiling. Taelann pushed aside a vegetable bin that blocked the entrance to the common room, then, testing each footstep, led Archos and Delmaria through the doorway. They paused beside the bar and scanned the destruction. The tables and chairs lay scattered around the room amid shattered glass and splintered planking. The hearth quietly sat in its corner. Cold ashes replaced the warmth of its blaze. This room had always given its visitors the feeling that they had come home, a feeling of peace and belonging. Today, chilled indifference served as the welcome to the three beside the bar. Beyond the broken windows, they could see that the buildings across the square had also suffered. Only the alchemist's shop remained undamaged. Shrugging off his shock, Archos slowly picked his way through the debris to the door. Taelann examined the room carefully, searching for signs of injuries and death. Delmaria remained beside the bar, her hand softly caressing its smooth surface. "There is no sign that anyone was injured," Taelann said,

returning to Delmaria. "I wonder where Stan is." Reluctantly, Delmaria removed her hand from the bar and followed the path Archos had taken to the square. "We need to find someone to tell us what happened," she muttered. Taelann followed her. They met Archos outside. The entire area looked as if someone had placed the town in a bone-rolling cup and given it a few good shakes. They were close to the wall that faced the canyon. Normally it would be visible above the shops and houses around the square. No sign of it could be detected. "It would take a great deal of magic to do this type of damage," Taelann observed. "I wonder why Ky's ward didn't prevent this." "I considered a magical attack as well. There are no traces of magic. The cause appears to have been natural," Archos answered. "Let's find someone and see what they have to say about this." Delmaria did not wait to see if Archos and Taelann followed her. She strode through the square to the road that would lead to the main thoroughfare of the town. Forlorn and silent, crippled shops and dwellings lined both sides of the dirt street watching the three intruders through gaping windows and slanting doorways. Some had thrown down pieces of planking and shingle. Some had spit shattered glass into the dust. Some still creaked on unsure footing, ready to add more debris to the wreckage-strewn path. Delmaria, Archos and Taelann began to hear the steady rhythm of shovels as they neared the front gates of Cragsguard. There, they found a small detachment of militia clearing the collapsed tower from the entrance and nearby road. Dark gray dust clung to their sweat-soaked backs as they worked. One of the men noticed them and set his shovel aside before walking to them. "My Lady. My Lords," he greeted as he bowed. "Stan wished you to know that he is at the manor seeing to those in need." "What happened?" Archos asked. "We believe it was an earthquake, My Lord. It happened last night. Luckily, only this end of town was hit by it. From what we can tell, the goblin caves and the canyon faired far worse." "Thank you," Archos said stroking his beard. "We'll head to the manor and see what help we can offer. If we see Stumpy, we'll send him down here to assist you. He has an affinity with earth and stone." "Lord Stumpy left town shortly after the earthquake hit, My Lord." The man bowed again and returned to his shovel. Archos,

Delmaria and Taelann headed up the road towards the manor. The farther they walked from the canyon, the less damage they detected. Taelann turned aside at the library. "I'll find you two later," he said as he left them. "Good luck. Send our regards to Daelann and Aemar, please." "I will," Taelann said as he entered the library courtyard. Archos and Delmaria arrived at the entrance to the manor. They found the courtyard nearly full of people. Shelters were being constructed along one side of the courtyard for those whose homes had been damaged. Meals were being prepared along the front wall of the manor itself. The stables were being extended to handle the extra animals that had been housed near the walls that had collapsed. They found Stan at the food preparation tables. "It figures. You two show up after all the hardest work is over with," Stan said smiling at them. "We may have come sooner had we known what happened," Delmaria answered as she hugged him. "Well, things got busy," Stan replied as he stirred the stew. "What happened? We know there was an earthquake, but the gentleman that gave us that information preferred the company of his shovel over us." Stan gazed upon the wooden spoon he held, then glanced at Archos. "Ask Maltar. He might part with his hammer long enough to speak with you about it." "Father!" Delmaria fumed. Stan laughed as he handed the spoon to the woman beside him and led Archos and Delmaria into the manor. More townsfolk meandered around the entry hall, most of them tending to the needs of the injured. Nine beds had been set up along the side wall for the injured. Stan walked past them and into a small alcove beneath the central stairway. Within, four comfortably padded chairs with faded red upholstery nestled around a small wooden table. When all were seated, Stan related the events. "It happened shortly after sunset, last night. We heard it before we saw it. Apparently, it began in the canyon occupied by the goblins. From what I've see of the canyon, I doubt many survived. Seconds later we felt it. The ground rumbled and shook. It didn't last long, no more than a few seconds. Stumpy muttered something about "Mother Stone" being angry and took his leave. No one has seen him since. "The Cracked Anvil was nearly full when it happened. Not one person at the inn was injured, in spite of all the broken glass and falling timbers. When we felt it was over, we went to see what damage had happened and to help those that needed it. From what I

can tell, only the nine you saw in the entry hall sustained injuries. Three of the guards that were on the wall died, having fallen into the canyon. The guards that fell inward received mostly scrapes and bruises. "I believe the ward Ky and I put up around the town saved quite a few lives. That little elf is amazing, don't you think?" Archos slowly stroked his beard and nodded agreement. "I'm sure that had something to do with the lack of life lost. From what we saw on our way here, I'd have guessed many more would be dead or seriously injured." "Archos and I can help with the reconstruction of the damaged homes with our magic," Delmaria said. "The sight of the Cracked Anvil cold and barren like that chilled me to the bone. I will start there." "Stumpy would be a great help with the outer wall, if he were here," Archos added. "I'm sure his skill with stone would make it considerably more resistant if "Mother Stone" were angered again." He leaned forward and asked Stan, "Do you remember an earthquake happening near here before?" "Nae," Stan replied. "This is the first I've experienced, and may it be the last." Delmaria and Archos stood. "If you need us, we'll be working on repairing the damage," Delmaria said. "Taelann will probably show up soon. He's in the library working on a different problem. Please let him know where we are." "You can trust me," Stan answered grinning. "What is this other problem he is working on?" "The children ran into some thantors in the Eldar forest," Archos explained. "Aemir did not do very well. Taelann is speaking with Daelann and Aemar to determine what kind of training he has had." Stan's grin disappeared as he stood. "They are fine," Delmaria said, smiling at him. "The triplets and Brek, a goblin Ky brought to the farm, fought well against them. Eleana handled the healing quite well." "Little Ky did well, also," Archos added. "He sustained some injuries but was still standing when the fighting had ceased." Stan smiled. "That boy is blood to me. His doing well makes me proud!" Archos patted Stan on the shoulder and said, "We are proud of all of them. You know where to find us if you need." Stan returned to his pot of stew as Delmaria and Archos returned to the Cracked Anvil. Weaving their spells slowly, they knew intuitively how to guide their magics to work as one. Before leaving

the Cracked Anvil, they made sure the hearth burned brightly. The feeling of home returned to the common room causing them to linger a moment before moving to the blacksmith's shop. They worked through the night. Shortly after dawn, Taelann joined them. "Come to help?" Archos asked as his magic righted a door. "I must return to the farm," Taelann said. "There seems to have been a bit of a problem at the Eldar village. Aemir asked that I send Tobit and Karnak there to assist them." "Let us know if you need us," Delmaria said. "This can wait a couple hours if need be." "I will. Good luck to you. I'll return to let you know what I learned after this is settled." Taelann left them and Archos and Delmaria returned to their work. They reached the main road as Stumpy came through the gap the guards had made in the collapsed front gate. The dwarf's beard and hair were covered in gray dust and his frown was deeper than either Archos or Delmaria had seen in many years. Behind Stumpy, a young female dwarf rushed to keep up with him. "Where might I be finding Stan?" Stumpy asked. "He's at the manor," Delmaria answered. "What did you find?" "Later," grumbled the dwarf. "After I rid myself of this waif!" The dwarf tramped up the main road at a quick pace with the child running behind him. Archos glanced at Delmaria and shrugged. "We've only a few more to go," Archos observed. "Let us finish this task. Then we will find our grumbling friend and get an explanation." "I agree. He will not be in the mood to tell his tale just yet," Delmaria said as she positioned herself in front of the next damaged building. "I think we'll need some of my father's ale to loosen his tongue." Archos grinned then prepared his spells for the task before him.

7 Ghostspawn studied the wall of dirt he had been attempting to dig through. He had been working a while and very little progress showed from his efforts. The pangs of hunger also began gnawing at him. This confused the goblin. Somehow, he thought immortality would erase the need for food. With one last scowl at the wall of rubble, he returned to the throne room. The fire had gone out long ago. Several of the corpses that once clogged the passageway lay in the fire-pit. Ghostspawn dragged them away then started a new fire with flint and some ragged clothing he removed from the dead goblins that kept him company. Once he had the wood burning well, he searched through the goblins to find one that would provide a suitable meal for himself. He dragged the corpse to the fire then retrieved the short-sword he kept behind his throne. He cut off the head and tossed it aside, then split open the goblin's abdomen and dug out the viscera with his hands. Then he rammed the spit downward through the chest cavity. He tied the arms and legs to the spit and lifted it into place above the fire. As he stood beside the fire turning the spit, he glanced at the ancient ghost symbol on the wall and thought back to his youth. After seeing The Ghost that first time, he became fascinated with the elf. For weeks he searched the network of underground caverns the goblins called home. Soon, he learned where all the symbols painted by the elf were located. Touching them caused him pain, but he sought them out anyway. He smirked as he remembered trying to find a pattern to The Ghost's visits. He never could find a

way to predict when or where The Ghost would appear next. He looked again at the symbol beside his throne. He had been chief of these goblins since that symbol first adorned the wall. It was also the last symbol The Ghost painted here. Almost two thousand years passed before The Ghost returned. Fat dripping into the fire from the corpse brought him back to the present. He paid better attention to his dinner, not wishing it to be ruined. When his meal was complete, he searched the corpses again until he found a scabbard for his short-sword. Then he wrapped a few pieces of meat in some rags he found and approached his throne. He needed a tool to dig with. He no longer needed the throne. Deciding this, he ripped one of the arms from the chair. The board was sturdy, about three inches thick and almost two feet long. Before heading to the tunnel, Ghostspawn placed his hand upon the symbol painted on the wall. It no longer pained him. He could feel the power though. He let his hand linger, drinking in the feeling for long moments, knowing this would be the last time. Finally, he turned away and walked down the passage. Stepping over the corpses of his tribe brought the cat-god to his mind. Ghostspawn muttered a curse and thought that the god might return to gloat over what he had done to the goblin. This thought quickened the goblin's pace. He did not want to be here if the cat-god returned. He began digging as soon as he reached the wall of rubble. His first plan was to follow the tunnels he knew so well. This changed when he decided that he probably would not recognize them filled with dirt and stone. Instead, he started digging upward at a steep angle. He let the dirt fill in the tunnel behind him feeling no need to return to his old home. He lost track of time. His hunger returned, but he ignored it, poking into the packed earth above his head with the board. The dirt would cascade down around him and he would push it downward to make room for the next wave. Hour after hour he dug. His arms ached, begging him to stop making them work. He paid them no heed. Inch by inch, he worked his way upward. Finally, after three days, the board broke the surface. Ghostspawn made the hole big enough for his head and cautiously searched the area before enlarging the hole so the rest of his body could escape. He emerged a hundred yards from the canyon. Cragsguard's walls stood silhouetted against the stars on the far side. He crept to some bushes on the canyon's edge and examined what once was the network of caves the goblins called home. He could find no evidence they were ever there. He remained hidden in the bushes and ate some of the meat he had brought with him. Having escaped, he wondered where he would go. From his

youth, he knew the road at the mouth of the canyon led to the elven kingdoms. He had seen elves coming from both directions on it. He was not fond of elves and knew they would not be fond of him. He had heard that the hobgoblins to the east had been killed but he did not trust what he heard. He knew they could not kill him, but his dig to the surface exhausted him and he did not want to encounter them. He decided to travel around the canyon and head west. His mind made up and having no desire to stay in the area where he might be found, he set out on his journey. He trusted the night to conceal him and would rest when this canyon was far behind him.

8 The students were standing quietly beside their seats by the time Herr William entered the dining hall. Many glanced his way as he walked to his place at the head table. It had been many years since he was the last to enter, long before any of these boys had attended the school. Usually, Herr William would be standing at the head table before the first of the boys arrived. He smiled as he read the emotions so blatantly etched on their young faces. Many showed concern, some showed amazement, the younger boys glanced his way with shy grins. Arriving at his place, he nodded and the hall filled with the song of grace. Herr William listened intently, knowing that soon he would hear it no longer. He waited a moment after the room silenced before seating himself. The students and other teachers followed him. Conversations in the dining hall had always been quiet, but tonight, they seemed to be more so. Herr William looked around the room and smiled at those who glanced his way. Then he scanned the teachers around him. His gaze stopped at an empty chair to his right. The place had been set and the wine poured, but the seat remained empty. The news of Micah's leaving had not made it to the majority of the school. Herr William quickly looked to his left where the other half of the faculty dined, again smiling at those that glanced his way. He turned his chair slightly and started a conversation with Herr Jensen who sat to his immediate left. He had just convinced himself that he would make it through the meal without his emotions alarming the students when he heard a quiet voice behind him. "Excuse me," the voice said. "Is this seat taken?"

"It is Herr Micah's seat, but I've not seen him today. If he arrives, I'm sure we will find another seat for him," answered the kindergarten teacher. "I don't believe he will be here tonight," the voice said as Herr William heard the sound of a chair being dragged across the floor. Herr William knew the voice well though he did not dare believe the owner was actually here. He turned slowly and looked down the table. At first, he thought his eyes and emotions were deceiving him. Then the Old Man smiled and raised his wine goblet to Herr William before taking a sip. Four faculty members sat between the Old Man and himself, making the rest of the meal last a dreadfully long time. Finally, the students sang their thanksgiving grace. Herr William hastily dismissed them and rushed to the Old Man's side. "It is so good to see you!" Herr William exclaimed. "I promised that I would visit," the Old Man explained. "Things have settled down quite a bit now. I doubt my brother, Karn- Rachk'sha will be causing any problems in the near future." "Come," Herr William said, leading the Old Man from the hall. "Let us go to the cottage so you can tell me all about it. How long will you be staying?" "I'm in no hurry to go anywhere," the Old Man replied. The Old Man began to tell his tale as they strolled through the gardens. They lingered between the two fountains where Ky's funeral ceremony had been held. The remnants of the pyre still remained in the center of the square. The Old Man took a golden box from his pocket and gathered some of the ashes into it. He secured the lid tightly before putting it away. Once at the cottage, the Old Man made tea and the two men settled in the front room as the Old Man related all that had happened at the farm. Herr William listened intently and asked several questions during the telling of the tale. "Micah must be thrilled to be training with elves and Little Ky," Herr William said, smiling. "I know very little of Ky's triplets,” the Old Man explained. “They were born while I was here in Austria. The short time that I had to observe them left me quite impressed. The youngest of the three looks exactly like Ky, except for the eyes. I'm told he acts like him, too." "So Micah is in good hands?" Herr William asked. The Old Man smiled. "Aye, very good hands. The eldest, Eleana is a healer. According to Tobit, a very good one at that. I know very little of the middle one except that his name is Tal. He seemed to be less unpredictable than his father and younger brother."

"The three of them, together, would make a good balanced team. Do they get along well?" The Old Man nodded. "From what I observed, they do. What has been happening here since I left? Are skateboards outlawed yet?" Herr William laughed and told the Old Man his plans. They talked until well past midnight. "Tell me you will be here tomorrow," Herr William said as he stood outside the door of the cottage. "I'll be here tomorrow and for a while after that if I am welcome," the Old Man replied, smiling. "You will always be welcome. Good night to you, Old Man." "Good night to you as well, my friend." The Old Man watched until Herr William passed from sight. Then he returned to the easy chair and looked for Brooks' The Talismans of Shannara, the book he had started before Ky released him from his brother's prison. Not finding it, he chose Split Infinity, by Piers Anthony from the shelf and began to read. The next few days were pleasant for both Herr William and the Old Man. During the day, Herr William concentrated on making everything ready for his retirement. The board had approved Herr Jensen's nomination and Herr William worked with him to make the transition smooth. Both of Herr William's choices for replacing Herr Jensen and Micah accepted their positions and their respective choirs were adjusting well. Meanwhile, the Old Man enjoyed his days in the garden. Two or three of the boys would visit him during the day. Little Ky's last group of friends were frequent visitors and wanted to know all about where he had gone and what he was doing. Herr William and the Old Man spent their evenings together. If they were not at the cottage sharing stories, they were attending a concert or play in town. On the fifth night, they returned from a Beethoven concert by the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra to find Ky seated on the sofa frowning at the portable CD player. Herr William's shoulders sagged at the sight of the young elf dressed in the choir boy uniform he had been given when he walked from the funeral pyre. "I guess it is time for you to leave again," Herr William muttered. "I don't believe so," replied the Old Man. "Let's ask him before we say our farewells, prematurely." The Old Man walked across the room with Herr William following. "It's good to see you again, my young friend," the Old Man said as he bowed. "What brings you to Vienna?"

"Why won't this make music?" Ky asked. The Old Man sat in the easy chair and glanced at the CD player and several pieces of bark Ky had placed on the table. "I think Herr William can bring that to life for you," the Old Man said. Ky frowned and glanced at Herr William then quickly looked away. "I'm sorry," he muttered. "I didn't know until he was gone." "Didn't know what?" Herr William asked. Ky looked at Herr William again. This time he held his gaze. "I didn't know he was your son. I would not have taken him if I had." Herr William nodded slowly, then smiled. "As long as Micah is happy, I am fine. It would be nice to see him again, though." He picked up the CD player and carried it to the shelf behind the sofa. "These work better if they are plugged into the wall. What music did you want to hear?" "When I was in the red haze," Ky explained, "there was music playing that kept me company. I think Little Ky played it for me, but I don't know what it was. I will know if I hear it again." "Try the Mozart disc," the Old Man said. "It was Little Ky's favorite." Ky arranged the bark as Herr William found the Mozart CD. Ky grinned as the music began. As each song ended, Ky carved a rune on the piece of bark in front of him and moved it to the side, replacing it with the next. At the end of the CD, Ky picked up the first piece and traced the rune. A red haze projected above the table, but no sound could be heard. He tried with each piece and had the same result. "Can you play it again?" he asked as he rearranged the bark on the table. Ky tried once more to record the memory of the music on the bark as it played. Herr William and the Old Man could feel his concentration as if it were a tangible item they could grasp but could not see. The results were the same as the first time. Ky sagged back onto the sofa, scowling at the bark while lightning danced across his fists. "What are you trying to do?" Herr William asked. Ky did not answer. He sat staring at the bark that had betrayed him. "He is trying to remember the music," the Old Man said, his voice quiet. "Long before language was written, the elves used the bark of dead branches to preserve the memory of important events. The first rune prepares the bark for the memory. The second one invokes the memory so that it can be seen and heard at a later time." "Why doesn't it work?" Ky asked.

"It works best with something you are familiar with. This music is very different from anything you would have heard before. It is also very complicated," the Old Man explained. "Maybe if it were simplified somewhat, it might work for you," Herr William said. "I could play some of these songs on the piano for you." "Will they be the same?" Ky asked. "The melody will be the same. Let's go down to the school and you can decide there," Herr William said. "His presence will probably cause a bit of excitement," the Old Man warned. "I doubt it will be any more exciting than his funeral was." The Old Man laughed, "You have a point there." As they walked to the school, Ky collected more bark. He had no faith in the bark he had used in the cottage and discarded it. The hour was late and they met no one as they progressed to the music room. Herr William procured the music for three of the Mozart compositions that were on the CD. Ky seated himself on the floor beside the piano and prepared the bark as Herr William waited. "I'm ready," Ky said. Herr William played the first song, "Ave Verum Corpus." He chose it because the melody was simple for a Mozart composition. When he finished, Ky tried to invoke the memory from the bark. This time, small snatches of the melody could be heard from the red haze that hovered over the bark. "Let me play it a couple times before you try to preserve the memory," Herr William suggested. "Sit up here with me and watch my hands. It might help if you use that as the visual part of the memory." Herr William played it three more times as Ky watched his fingers dance across the keys. After the third time, Ky slid off the seat and picked up a piece of bark. He placed it at the end of the keyboard where he knew Herr William's hand would not go. "Play it one more time before I try to remember it," Ky said. "I want to try something." Herr William began playing the song again. This time, Ky added his voice to Herr William's right hand. Herr William had been at the choir school for over fifty years. In that time, he had heard many very talented voices. None affected him as Ky's did. His hands faltered midway through the song, distracted by the haunting magic in the young elf's voice. "I'm sorry," he murmured as he brushed the tears from his eyes. "I have never heard anything so wonderful before. Please, let me try again." If Herr William had not played this melody hundreds of

times, he would not have gotten through it. He had to remind himself to breathe when the last note faded from the room. Ky waited patiently for Herr William to collect himself to play the song one more time. The memory rune had been carved into the bark and Ky was confident that this time it would work. Herr William played it again, the memory of Ky's voice guiding his hands. Afterwards, Ky invoked the memory. Herr William's right hand projected above the piano as the notes rang clearly through the room. Ky grinned and carefully placed the memory bark into a pouch he wore at his waist. "Please," Herr William requested, "sing it for the school tomorrow. I will play for you if you would grace us with your voice." Ky grinned. "You have given me something that will bring me peace for a long time. I will do as you ask." "I believe I would have trouble playing the other melodies tonight. We will try again tomorrow night if you wish." Ky placed his hand on the side of Herr William's head. "When you wish me to sing, call me and I will come to you. Until then, I'll be in the woods." He slid off the bench and left. Herr William turned to the Old Man who was seated behind him. "I had no idea that he could sing like that." The Old Man smiled and said, "He's a full blood elf. With very few exceptions, they all sing like that. You should hear when they sing together." "If only I could." Herr William put the music away and walked with the Old Man to the cottage. "Good night, Old Man." "Good night to you as well, Herr William." Herr William took his time returning to the school. He listened, as if it were the first time in his life, to the sounds of the woodlands around him. He felt the pulse of the earth and the breath of the tall Austrian Pines that he walked beneath. The pale moonlight bathed his surroundings in a soft glow. Halfway down the path, he saw Ky waiting ahead of him. The sight of the elf in this environment sent his mind back to the childhood tales of fairies and other magical woodland creatures. He smiled, remembering that as a child, he always wanted to find one, to know they were real. "I was wondering," Ky whispered when Herr William stopped before him, "can you arrange a song for me to hear tomorrow?" "What song would you like to hear?" "At my spirit sending, I heard many voices singing the song of safe travel to my spirit. I had to stop it then, though I didn't want

to. I would like to hear it, now that it won't send my spirit away from me." Herr William smiled. "That I can arrange. Rest well, young elf." "You too," Ky said disappearing from Herr William's sight. Herr William almost stayed in the woods that night. The moonlight acted the part of the legendary willow wisps that led travelers away to be hopelessly lost forever. He thought he would be content to be lost forever. Something in the elven song made him feel more alive than he had ever felt before. His feet continued towards the school though, denying him the chance to be led astray. He looked forward to the rising of the sun on the new day, knowing he would hear the majesty of elven song once more. The next morning, Herr William prepared the choirs to sing "The Song of Spirit Sending" that they had learned for Ky's funeral. The choristers rehearsed for an hour and Herr William was very pleased with the results. Afterwards, he asked what they knew of elven song. He was pleased to see that many of the students had read stories that mentioned the beauty of elven voices. He promised that they would hear it for themselves after they sang the song they rehearsed. After lunch, he assembled the choirs in the school's concert hall, then called for Ky. The elf appeared at Herr William's side immediately. The choirs were arranged in the same formation as they had been for the funeral. Ky's chair sat in the center. When Ky was seated, Herr William signaled Herr Jensen to begin. Herr William noticed the small piece of bark in Ky's hand and hoped the memory would be recorded properly for him. As the last notes drifted away, Ky sat with his eyes closed, his breathing slow and easy as if he were sleeping. A few moments of silence followed before Ky whispered, "Thank you." Herr William waited as the choristers quietly took their seats in the hall, then sat at the piano. Ky climbed onto the bench beside him. Once again, Herr William played the Mozart song, "Ave Verum Corpus," and Ky sang it. Everybody in the room was enthralled by the music. They all knew the song, though none, save Herr William, had heard it performed quite like this. As soon as the song ended, Ky picked up his piece of bark and vanished. The choristers left the hall silently, many with wide eyes and mouths agape. Neither Herr William nor the Old Man saw Ky until late that evening. They had gone to the practice room because Herr William wanted to practice the next Mozart song, "Alleluja." They found Ky waiting for them there. This night's composition was more complicated. There were parts of the song that Ky had great difficulty

grasping. He sang with the parts he learned and listened intently to the troublesome parts. Two boys heard the music as they passed down the hall and hid outside the door to listen. Ky knew they were there, but said nothing. After a couple hours of working through the song, Herr William became tired and started making mistakes. "We will try again tomorrow night," Ky said, softly. He vanished before Herr William had a chance to agree or disagree. "I wish I could do that," Herr William said to the Old Man as they left the room. The Old Man laughed. "He does a lot of things I wish I could do as well." They walked down the hall past the two boys hiding in the shadows. When the two men were gone, the boys crept to their dormitory. "They will be there tomorrow night. You want to go again?" the first boy whispered. "Try to stop me," the second answered as he climbed into bed. Ky remained scarce the next day. He was not in the practice hall when Herr William and the Old Man arrived. Herr William decided to practice a little before the elven voice was there to distract him. Outside in the hall, the two boys were already hiding behind a tapestry. They listened while Herr William played the song, anxiously awaiting the elven singing they yearned to hear. "It would be easier to hear if you were in there with us," a quiet voice said. Both boys jumped, nearly ripping the tapestry from the wall. They had neither seen nor heard Ky approach and yet he stood with them behind the tapestry. Ky grinned at them, "Come on. You can listen inside." They followed Ky through the door, eyes wide with terror as they anticipated the punishment that would be given them by Herr William. "I found them behind the tapestry," Ky explained. "They will be able to hear better in here. Don't you think?" Herr William laughed. "Yes. I don't blame them for wanting to hear either." This was Herr William's last week at the school. Each day, the preparations for his retirement progressed. Each night, the memory sessions continued. The two boys were given permission to listen since Herr William knew that they would be hiding outside the room regardless. By the end of the week, Ky had managed to preserve two more songs, "Alleluja" and "Dies Irae" on bark. He did not vanish

as he usually did after the last session. Instead, he walked with Herr William and the Old Man to the cottage. "Where do you plan on going?" the Old Man asked. "I've been looking for an apartment. I haven't found one yet, but I can stay at the school until I do find one," Herr William answered. "You have been a big help to me," Ky said. "If you could have one wish, what would it be?" "I would see my son again," Herr William answered without hesitation. Ky glanced at the Old Man, then said, "There are no pianos there." Herr William laughed, "Is there perchance an apartment available?" Ky stopped. Herr William and the Old Man stopped and turned to look at him. "Consider your wish carefully, Herr William." Ky pointed at the Old Man. "Talk with him before you decide. I will ask you again tomorrow." Ky vanished. The Old Man and Herr William walked to the cottage without speaking. When they arrived, Herr William made himself comfortable on the sofa as the Old Man made tea. They talked about Herr William's options until dawn lightened the room. The Old Man insisted that Herr William sleep at the cottage. He would need rest to speak with Ky about his wishes. When Herr William woke early that afternoon, the Old Man made him breakfast. They talked more about Herr William's desires. Ky did not appear as the day drifted into evening. Herr William felt the urge to visit the woods. The moon was full and he wanted to see if the same magic he experienced a week before would still be there. The Old Man walked with him. They walked for close to an hour before they found Ky. "Your possessions are in your new apartment," Ky whispered. "Tasenta can take you there when you are ready." Ky faded slightly, then became solid again. "I hope the school will not miss that piano." He grinned and vanished. Herr William stared at the spot Ky had stood. "He already knew?" The Old Man smiled, "He knew yesterday when you told him. He wanted to make sure you knew. Let us continue our walk." They left the path that led to the school and entered the woodlands. The pine needles cushioned their footsteps and the moonlight guided them. Herr William felt younger, energetic, as if he could walk all night long. Within the hour, they found a dirt road that

Herr William had never seen before. They followed the road that led them up the side of a canyon. Soon, they could see part of a stone wall rising before them. They walked through the crumbled entryway and turned right at the first street in the town. The Old Man guided Herr William to a small square, then into a tavern. It felt like home. A warm fire burned brightly in the hearth and the room was filled with the sounds of pleasant conversation and laughter. The Old Man walked to the end of the bar and sat, followed by Herr William. "Evening, Stan. Two ales, please." Stan smiled and placed two ales on the bar. "A newcomer to town," he said looking at Herr William. "I feel a good tale about to be told." At a small table in the back corner, Ky smiled as he ate the meal his adopted grandfather had made for him.

9 Ky II had stepped away from the group, his body engulfed in white flames. Tal and Eleana continued to back away from the barricade. They could sense their brother's anger and kept their thoughts quiet. The smoke from the burning barricade blinded the elves in the village to Ky II's approach until he pushed through the blazing barrier and entered the small stream. Ky II did not have Simon's spirit vision, but he knew how to set up sentries to protect an area. He stopped on the far bank of the stream and searched each of the nearby trees. He could not see the elves, but he knew they would not know that. He stared into each tree for the moment where he thought a sentry might be hidden, giving the impression that he had spotted them. When he spoke, his voice was quiet and menacing as it drifted from his flame encased body with an edge of insanity to it. "Since last night, I've been attacked by thantors, seen four of my friends lying near death as a result, had my quest for sey hides denied because there weren't enough left to clothe my companions, and now, when we come to our own people's village, we get shot at with arrows. I want someone here to speak with me face to face or I will burn this village and all in it to the ground." He paused and scanned the trees one more time, then added, "I'm not going to wait long." He glimpsed the elf that dropped to the ground from one of the trees in front of him and heard its footfalls as he ran into the village. A moment later, an elder female approached him. She carried herself regally. A circlet of gold kept her long silver hair from her

green eyes. Ky II smiled slightly, seeing the apprehension within her eyes. She stopped ten paces from him and bowed. "My apologies for the lack of welcome," she said. "Our lives are under constant threat from the thantors recently. What need brings you here?" "We only seek to trade for some sey hides, then we will be on our way." "You claim that you were attacked by thantors. How is it you survived? You are but a small group of children." -Bring the thantor heads to me- Ky II thought to Tal. "We have had training. I believe you are calling me a liar." Ky II saw her expression change immediately. He knew he had guessed correctly. He took a step forward. "You almost make me ashamed to be an Eldar elf," he whispered. He made a quick gesture with his left hand and watched the female cringe. Instead of the attack she expected, Ky II had doused his flame as Tal approached. -Dump them at her feet.- Ky II thought to Tal. He watched her closely as Tal dumped the bundle on the ground at the female's feet. She gasped and backed away from the grotesque trophies. Slowly, she tore her gaze from the heads littering the path and stared at Ky II. "I've seen you before. You are the demon child, but your eyes are not what I expected." She glanced at Tal and added, "I did not know you had a brother." "I believe you have mistaken my brother for my father," Tal corrected. "He isn't here. He's busy killing thantors somewhere else at the moment." "I have one more question for you before I invite you into the village. You mentioned that four of your friends are near death. Where are they now?" -Bring everyone in.- Ky II thought to Eleana. "They are here with us. My sister is a healer, and she's very good at it." The female watched as Eleana led Micah, Little Ky, Brek, Aemir and Simon across the stream. She walked around the thantor heads and approached Micah. She nodded then lifted aside one of the rents in his blood-stained tunic to observe the wound. "You are indeed a talented healer," she said turning to Eleana. "You may leave here with all the hides you need and any provisions that you wish to take if you can perform your art on one that lies near death as we speak." "I will do all I can," Eleana answered. The female raised her right arm and four elven guards

appeared on the path. "Take the children to the common hall and see that they are well fed." She turned to Eleana, "Follow me, please. I will take you to young Aprean." Eleana followed the female through the village to a small cottage not far from the center commons. The front room was dimly lit and Eleana could barely make out the simple but comfortable furnishings. She was led to a small room with two pallets along opposite walls. A young elf lay unnaturally still on one of them. "This is my son. He was attacked, like you and your friends, by thantors. These creatures are new to us.
